headline: Uber Founder's New Company Might Build Self-Driving Taxis

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Travis Kalanick started a famous company called Uber a long time ago. Now he has a new company called Atoms. This summer, Atoms got a huge amount of money, $1.7 billion, from investors who believe in the company. That is a giant pile of cash used to help a business grow. People wondered what Atoms would actually build. Now we know more. Atoms wants to work on 'robotaxis.' A robotaxi is a car that drives itself, without a human driver, and can pick people up like a taxi. Atoms has even talked with Uber about using its self-driving technology. Uber already gave Atoms $100 million to help. Atoms also bought a smaller company called Pronto, which builds self-driving machines for mining. Pronto's leader once worked at Uber but got in trouble for taking secret information from another company. He was later forgiven by the president. This story matters because self-driving cars could change how people travel in the future, maybe even in your town someday.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Travis Kalanick, the man who created Uber, now runs a different company called Atoms. Back in the summer, Atoms raised $1.7 billion from investors, including a major firm called Andreessen Horowitz. Raising money like this is called a 'funding round,' and it helps new companies grow by hiring workers and building products. At first, nobody was sure exactly what Atoms planned to make. Now, a news report says Atoms is getting ready to hire many new employees and buy other companies so it can become a big name in self-driving cars, also called autonomous vehicles. Atoms has even discussed with Uber how Uber might use Atoms' robotaxi technology. A robotaxi is a car that can drive passengers around without a human behind the wheel. Uber has already invested $100 million into Atoms, showing it takes this partnership seriously. Uber also works with several other self-driving car companies already. Atoms recently bought a company called Pronto, which makes self-driving equipment for mining sites. Pronto's boss used to lead Uber's self-driving car team, but he was convicted for stealing secret business information from a competitor. He was sentenced to prison time but was later pardoned, meaning his punishment was officially canceled, by President Trump. This story is important because it shows how self-driving technology keeps expanding into transportation, and it could shape how people get around cities in the years ahead.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Travis Kalanick, best known for founding Uber, now leads a newer company called Atoms. In the summer, Atoms announced it had raised $1.7 billion in a funding round, meaning investors gave the company that much money in exchange for a stake in its future success. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, a well-known venture capital firm that invests in promising startups. At the time, Kalanick did not clearly explain what Atoms planned to build, which left many people curious. Now, according to a report from the Financial Times, Atoms is preparing to hire large numbers of employees and acquire other companies as it pushes into the autonomous vehicle industry, meaning technology for vehicles that can drive themselves without human control. One major detail is that Atoms has already discussed with Uber how Uber could use Atoms' robotaxi technology in its ride-hailing service. A robotaxi is essentially a self-driving car used to transport passengers, similar to a taxi but without a driver. Uber has invested $100 million into Atoms directly, on top of already partnering with several other self-driving companies. This suggests Uber wants to stay closely connected to advances in self-driving technology, even though it isn't building the cars itself. Adding to this picture, Atoms recently acquired a company called Pronto, which builds autonomous technology for mining operations. Pronto is led by Anthony Levandowski, who once headed Uber's own self-driving car division. Levandowski was previously convicted of stealing trade secrets, which means he took confidential business information from a rival company without permission. He was sentenced to 18 months in prison, but he received a pardon, an official forgiveness of his crime, from President Donald Trump. This connects Atoms to a controversial figure but also to expertise in autonomous systems. Together, these details reveal that Atoms is quietly building toward a future where self-driving technology plays a central role in transportation and industries like mining, backed by serious money and experienced (if controversial) leadership.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Travis Kalanick, the entrepreneur who co-founded Uber, currently runs a company called Atoms, and new reporting suggests it may be moving toward the self-driving car industry. Earlier this summer, Atoms announced it had closed a massive funding round worth $1.7 billion, led by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. A funding round is when investors provide money to a company in exchange for partial ownership, betting that the business will grow and eventually become valuable. At the time, Kalanick was vague about Atoms' specific goals, describing his motivations only as 'unfinished business,' a phrase that hinted at ambitions tied to his earlier career at Uber. Now, a report from the Financial Times fills in some gaps. It says Atoms is preparing for a hiring spree and a series of acquisitions that could position it as a significant player in the autonomous vehicle industry, referring to technology that allows vehicles to operate without human drivers. Notably, Atoms has reportedly discussed with Uber the possibility of Uber using Atoms' robotaxi technology within its ride-hailing platform. A robotaxi is a self-driving vehicle designed to carry passengers much like a traditional taxi, but without a driver behind the wheel. This is not Uber's first move into this space; the company has already partnered with numerous other autonomous vehicle developers. Uber has also invested $100 million directly into Atoms, a figure that had been previously confirmed. While people familiar with Atoms' plans stress that robotaxis are not the company's only focus, this direction lines up with the ambitious tone Kalanick set when describing the funding round. Further supporting this trajectory, Atoms recently acquired Pronto, a startup focused on autonomous technology for the mining industry. Pronto is led by Anthony Levandowski, who previously served as Uber's head of self-driving car development. Levandowski's history is notable and complicated: he was convicted of stealing trade secrets, meaning he unlawfully took confidential information from a competing company, and was sentenced to 18 months in prison. However, he was later pardoned by President Donald Trump, officially clearing his criminal record. This combination of massive funding, high-profile partnerships, and experienced but controversial leadership suggests Atoms is positioning itself to become an influential force in how self-driving technology develops across transportation and industrial sectors in the coming years.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Travis Kalanick, who co-founded and once led Uber before departing the company in 2017, now runs a venture called Atoms, and recent reporting indicates the company may be steering toward autonomous vehicles, an industry closely tied to his past. In the summer, Atoms revealed that it had raised $1.7 billion in a funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz, one of Silicon Valley's most prominent venture capital firms. A funding round of this scale signals strong investor confidence, since venture capital firms provide large sums of money to startups in exchange for equity, essentially betting that the company's value will rise substantially over time. Despite the enormous investment, Kalanick offered little clarity about Atoms' actual mission, referring cryptically to 'unfinished business,' a phrase widely interpreted as a nod to ambitions he did not fully realize during his Uber tenure. A newer report from the Financial Times sheds more light on the situation, indicating that Atoms is preparing for an aggressive hiring campaign and a wave of acquisitions intended to establish it as a major competitor within the autonomous vehicle sector, the broader industry focused on vehicles capable of operating without human drivers through sensors, software, and artificial intelligence. Perhaps the most telling detail is that Atoms has reportedly held discussions with Uber about integrating Atoms' robotaxi technology into Uber's existing ride-hailing platform. A robotaxi refers to a self-driving vehicle designed specifically to transport paying passengers autonomously, functioning much like a conventional taxi but without a human operator. This would not be an isolated move for Uber, which has already formed partnerships with a range of other autonomous vehicle developers as it hedges its bets on which self-driving technologies will ultimately succeed. Uber has also placed a direct financial stake in Atoms, investing $100 million, a figure independently confirmed by TechCrunch, underscoring how seriously Uber views the potential partnership. Sources close to the matter caution that robotaxis represent only one component of Atoms' broader strategy rather than its sole focus, yet this direction aligns naturally with the expansive vision Kalanick has hinted at surrounding the funding round. Reinforcing this trajectory is Atoms' recent acquisition of Pronto, a startup specializing in autonomous technology for mining operations. Pronto is led by Anthony Levandowski, a figure well known in the self-driving world for previously heading Uber's own autonomous vehicle division. Levandowski's career took a controversial turn when he was convicted of stealing trade secrets, unlawfully taking proprietary technical information from a rival self-driving company, and was sentenced to 18 months in prison. He was later granted a pardon by President Donald Trump, formally absolving him of the conviction. Bringing Levandowski's expertise, along with substantial financial backing and Uber's interest, into Atoms suggests Kalanick may be assembling the pieces to reenter the autonomous vehicle race at a significant scale, with implications for ride-hailing, freight, and industrial automation alike.

questions: If self-driving taxis became common in your town, how do you think it would change the way you or your family get around?

Anthony Levandowski was convicted of a crime but later pardoned and is now leading a company again. Do you think people should get a second chance to work in the same industry after being convicted of a crime? Why or why not?

Big companies like Uber are investing huge amounts of money into self-driving technology. What are some good things and some risks that could come from more of our transportation being controlled by computers instead of people?
